transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bothering you or what brought you in to see me?

Well, thanks for having me. I, uh, I guess what brings me in is just this feeling... it’s like I’m constantly running on a motor lately. And I mean a literal motor, like one of those old two-stroke engines that just won't quit sputtering and revving. I teach special education, you know, and my days are already packed. I mean, from the moment the bell rings at 7:30 to when the last bus pulls away, it’s just go, go, go. But even after that, it’s like I can’t shut off. I’ll finish one thing at school, like putting away the sensory bins or grading IEP goals, and then I immediately jump into the next thing. And then I get home, and my wife is like, "Sit down, have a cup of coffee," but I can't. I'm fixing the hinge on the cabinet, then I'm out in the yard pulling weeds that don't even need pulling, then I'm reorganizing the garage shelves. It’s exhausting, honestly. I’m 58 years old, I shouldn’t be bouncing off the walls like one of my middle schoolers, but I just... I never seem to be able to shut myself off. It’s like the switch is broken in the "on" position, and I just keep going until I practically collapse, but even then, my brain is still buzzing about what I need to do the next day.
Is this restless, motor-like energy something new that started recently, or has it been a pattern you've noticed throughout most of your life?

Oh, no, no, no. Definitely not new. It’s funny you ask that, actually, because my wife was just saying she thought maybe it was the stress of getting older, or maybe related to some recent family changes we've had, but I had to tell her—and I've told her this a hundred times—this is just who I am. It’s who I’ve *always* been. I mean, if you could ask my mother, she would have had an absolute field day with that question. 

She used to tell this joke to practically everyone we met. She’d say that even back in elementary school, I practically taught the class from my seat. Or, well, I guess *not* from my seat, because the whole point of the joke was that I was literally always out of my chair. I just couldn't stay put for the life of me. I remember being in, gosh, maybe third or fourth grade, and I’d just be up, wandering around, talking to the kid next to me, or leaning over to talk to the kid three rows down. And the poor teachers... I would just cut right in before they even finished giving the directions. Like, they’d get halfway through saying what we were supposed to do, and I’d already be shouting out a question or jumping ahead to the next thing because I just couldn't wait for them to get to the end of the sentence. 

So, yeah, this restless thing... this is deeply ingrained. It was a huge part of who I was long, long before adulthood. It certainly isn't something that just started up recently with any family stuff or work stress. It’s just... it's been my normal since I was a little kid, which is ironic now that I'm the one standing at the front of the classroom trying to keep kids in their seats, you know? But yeah, always been this way. Always running.

Aside from this restless, motor-like energy, have you also noticed problems with things like staying focused on tasks, following through on details, or frequently losing track of things, both as a child and now as an adult?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because when you think about someone who's always on the go, always moving, you'd think they'd be scattered all over the place, right? Like a tornado just blowing through the room and leaving a mess everywhere. And I've definitely had colleagues over the years who fit that description—teachers who can't find their lesson plans or who forget to submit their attendance on time. I remember this one guy, Dave, taught physical education, nice guy, but he would lose his keys at least three times a week. We'd all be out in the parking lot helping him look for them. 

But for me... no, not really. I mean, I don't have those kinds of problems. I've never really been the type to lose my keys or forget what I'm supposed to be doing. Actually, it's almost the opposite in some ways. Because I'm always moving, I'm always *doing* the things that need to be done. Like, if I'm grading those IEP goals I mentioned earlier, I'll sit down—well, maybe not sit down, maybe I'll stand at the kitchen counter—and I'll power through them. I don't drift off or start daydreaming about my next vacation or anything like that. I stay right on it until it's finished. And then, boom, I'm onto the next thing. 

Even when I was a kid, you know, the teachers would get frustrated because I was out of my seat or talking out of turn, but it wasn't because I didn't know what was going on or because I'd lost my pencil or forgot the assignment. I knew exactly what was going on. I was usually just bored because I'd already finished it or I already knew the answer. I remember my fifth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was a real stickler for neatness—she used to check our desks every Friday to make sure they were organized. And mine was always perfectly fine. All my folders were there, my pencils were in the little box. I just couldn't sit still at the desk, that was the issue. 

So, yeah, focusing on the details or keeping track of things? That's never really been my struggle. I mean, my wife might say I focus *too* much on certain details sometimes, like when I was fixing that cabinet hinge and I spent twenty minutes making sure it was perfectly level even though it's just a laundry room cabinet that nobody ever looks at. But losing track of things or not following through? No, I wouldn't say I have any trouble with that at all. It's really just the constant, relentless need to be doing something, moving, talking, fixing... just always, always in motion.
Do you still find yourself interrupting conversations, finishing other people's sentences, or having trouble waiting your turn in line or in discussions now as an adult?

Oh boy. Yeah. That... that is probably the thing that gets me in the most hot water these days, to be completely honest with you. I don't do it to be rude, I really don't. I just... my brain moves so fast, and I see where the conversation is going, or I see the solution to whatever they are talking about, and I just sort of launch myself right in. 

Like, at school, if I hear two of my colleagues in the hallway trying to figure out a schedule change, or even if I am in a meeting with parents—which, as a special ed teacher, I have a lot of parent meetings—I will just jump right into the middle of their conversation. I always think I am helping! I just figure I have the answer to this, let me just save everyone some time and get it out there. But then I end up completely talking over them, or I just take charge of the whole discussion before they have even had a chance to finish their thought.

Has this constant need to move and jump into conversations actually caused ongoing problems for you—like conflicts with colleagues, tension with your wife, or issues at work—or is it more something people just notice about you without it causing real problems?

I wish... I really wish it was just a quirky thing people noticed, you know? Like, "Oh, there he goes, always in a rush, always talking." But... no. No, it's actually causing some very real, very heavy problems for me right now. It’s definitely not just something people brush off anymore. 

Just recently—well, it’s been building up for a while, I suppose, but it finally came to a head at school. I mentioned how I jump into those parent meetings and colleagues' conversations, right? Well, apparently, some of my co-teachers and the related service providers—like the speech pathologist and the school psychologist—they felt so completely steamrolled by me that they actually went to administration. They filed formal complaints. I was... I was completely blindsided by it. I thought we were a team and I was just keeping things moving efficiently! But the principal pulled me into his office, shut the door, and... well, they actually put me on a formal corrective plan. A corrective plan! After all my years of teaching! I have to have these documented check-ins now about "professional collaboration" and letting others speak. It’s humiliating, honestly. Because I’m really just trying to help! I see the solution and I want to get it out there to fix the issue, but instead... I feel like I'm completely damaging the trust with my colleagues. They look at me differently now. 

And it’s not just at school, either. It’s bleeding into my marriage, into my home life, too. I mentioned earlier that we've had some recent family changes—we've taken on some heavy caregiving responsibilities at home lately. It's a lot of work, a lot of moving parts, coordinating schedules and all that. And you'd think my energy would be a bonus, right? Like, "Great, he can run around and get everything done!" But my wife... she sat me down the other night, looking just completely exhausted, and she told me that my constant moving around, my pacing, my jumping in and taking over tasks she's already halfway through... she said it actually makes the caregiving routines so much harder for her. 

She told me, point-blank, that she feels like she has to manage *my* energy on top of everything else we are dealing with. That... man, that really stung. Because, again, I’m just trying to help! I want to lighten the load for her. But instead, I'm making her feel overwhelmed, and I can see the tension just radiating off her when I walk into the room sometimes.
